note: Human rulings that a specific comparison is undecidable under the current rubric. A ruled comparison is neither a match nor a miss: it is reported as its own category so a genuinely undecidable case is never silently counted as either. Rulings are frozen; add entries, do not edit them.
changes_from_v1: Rulings are keyed by (obligation_id, candidate_id, level) rather than obligation_id alone. The documented ambiguity is a property of a *relationship* — a candidate asking for a prerequisite of the maintainer's change — not of the obligation, so an obligation-wide key over-applied it to every other candidate that happened to reach the same obligation.

`level` distinguishes issue-level from resolution-level ambiguity. v1 applied its ruling to issue recall only; resolution recall ignored the registry entirely, which made `resolution_recall > issue_recall` reachable even though the two-level design says it is impossible.
`candidate_id: "*"` preserves an obligation-wide ruling where that is genuinely what was meant. The migrated v1 entry uses it, because its rationale names a class of candidates rather than one.

Rubric v9 adds a judge-emitted `abstain` verdict. That does not retire this registry: an abstention is the judge declining, while a ruling is a human deciding the rubric cannot settle the case. They are reported separately.

policy.denominator: Ambiguous comparisons stay in the obligation denominator and are reported separately. They are NOT excluded, because excluding them would inflate recall by removing the hardest cases.
policy.obligation_status: An obligation is `hit` if it issue-matches through at least one comparison that is not ruled ambiguous; `ambiguous` if its only issue-matching comparisons are ruled; `miss` otherwise. A ruled obligation with no issue-match is still a miss — the ruling governs how a match is counted, not whether one occurred.
policy.levels: A resolution-level ruling applies only to resolution scoring. An issue-level ruling propagates to resolution, because resolution is defined as conditional on issue: if it is undecidable whether the candidate names the same issue, it cannot be decidable whether its fix resolves it.

rulings.gold_claim: In `coveringNumber_le_packingNumber`, replace the manual `by_cases` proof with the `by_cases!` pattern and use `encard_maximalSeparatedSet` together with `IsCover.coveringNumber_le_encard`.
rulings.rationale: Candidates ask to rename `card_maximalSeparatedSet` to `encard_maximalSeparatedSet` and update downstream uses. Because the gold ask's own text names the renamed form, the requested proof rewrite presupposes the rename — the candidate requests a prerequisite of the maintainer's change rather than the change itself. Whether a prerequisite counts as the same issue is not settled by the rubric: 'a different fix may still issue-match' points one way, 'a rename when the ask is a proof change is false' points the other. Both v7.1 and v8 returned issue=True 3/3 on this pair, with reasoning that is defensible either way, so it is not judge noise.
rulings.scope_note: Kept obligation-wide (`candidate_id: "*"`) because the rationale names a class of candidates — all of those asking for the prerequisite rename — rather than one specific candidate. New rulings should name the candidate.

candidates_for_ruling.gold_claim: In `coveringNumber_two_mul_le_externalCoveringNumber`, replace the `rcases Set.eq_empty_or_nonempty A` split with `(rfl | h_nonempty)` and discharge the empty case by `simp`.
candidates_for_ruling.why: Candidates argue the split is dead code because `h_nonempty` is unused and propose removing it. Same rubric tension as the ruled entry, and the judge split its own samples 2-of-3 on it under v7.1 — the empirical signature of ambiguity. It is also one of the two pairs that carried v8's resolution-level splits, so a ruling here directly affects whether resolution recall is quotable. Not ruled: awaiting a human decision.
